t.7.47.1: Having heard the dreadful words of Lakṣmaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, Vaidehī, fell into the deepest despair and collapsed to the ground.
t.7.47.2: She, the daughter of Janaka, remained as if senseless for a moment, her eyes clouded with tears, and then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa in a wretched voice.
t.7.47.3: Surely, Lakṣmaṇa, this body of mine was created by the Creator for sorrow alone, since today sorrow itself in embodied form appears thus before me.
t.7.47.4: What sin, I wonder, was committed in the past, or who was parted from his wife, that I, a faithful wife of pure conduct, have been abandoned by the king?
t.7.47.5: Formerly, O Saumitri, following at Rāma's feet, I willingly accepted a dwelling in the hermitage, even though I was caught up in sorrow.
t.7.47.6: How, gentle one, shall I, thus left alone and deserted, dwell in the hermitage? And to whom shall I, wholly given over to sorrow, tell my grief?
t.7.47.7: And what shall I say among the sages? What wrong have I done to the king? Or for what reason have I been abandoned by the great-souled Rāghava?
t.7.47.8: Surely, O Saumitri, I will not cast off my life this very day in the waters of the Jāhnavī, for then the royal line of my husband would be lost.
t.7.47.9: Do as you have been commanded, Saumitri, and abandon me, a woman destined for sorrow. Let the king's command be obeyed, and hear these words of mine.
t.7.47.10: With joined palms and with due reverence, bowing your head at the feet of my mothers-in-law alike, without distinction, convey my wishes for his welfare to the king.
t.7.47.11: As you would conduct yourself toward your brothers, so should you always conduct yourself toward the citizens. For this would be the highest dharma, and this the unsurpassed glory.
t.7.47.12: O king, may you win over the people of the city through righteousness. I do not grieve for my own body, O bull among men, so much as for the censure of the citizens, O delight of the Raghus.
t.7.47.13: As Sītā was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, his spirit downcast, bowed his head to the ground and could not utter a word.
t.7.47.14: And having circumambulated her, he, still weeping with a loud cry, boarded the boat again and urged the boatman on.
t.7.47.15: Having reached the northern bank, he, weighed down by a burden of grief and as if bewildered by sorrow, quickly mounted the chariot.
t.7.47.16: Turning back again and again, Lakṣmaṇa saw Sītā writhing on the far bank like one without a protector, and then he departed.
t.7.47.17: Seeing the chariot standing far away, Sītā, distressed, gazed again and again at Lakṣmaṇa, and grief overcame her.
t.7.47.18: Bowed down by the weight of her sorrow, that glorious and virtuous lady, pitiable in her plight and no longer seeing her protector, wept with a loud cry in the forest that resounded with the calls of peacocks, being wholly overcome by grief.
